text: A statewide radio project needed 836 license-plan reports.
say: A statewide radio project needed eight hundred and thirty-six license-plan reports.

text: Each one is a PDF, built from the results of the project's studies.
The project held 185,161 studies and over eight million results.
say: The project held a hundred and eighty-five thousand, one hundred and sixty-one studies and over eight million results.

text: One plan took more than ten minutes, because it scanned the whole results table, over a billion rows.
Scanning twice per plan, one at a time, all 836 would have taken about 280 hours.
say: Scanning twice per plan, one at a time, all eight hundred and thirty-six would have taken about two hundred and eighty hours.

text: First I measured where a plan's time went, and most of it was loading results.
So each plan now finds its studies first and reads only their results, not the whole table.

say: One plan dropped to twenty point eight seconds.

text: Then one pass over the studies finds the results for every plan at once.
Each contour is prepared once, instead of once for every licensee it's checked against.
Instead of adding a proposed eight-gigabyte index, I narrowed what each plan reads.
Then one background job builds the plans sixteen at a time.
It shows progress, lists any failure by plan, and can be cancelled.
All 836 plans finished in about twelve minutes.
say: All eight hundred and thirty-six plans finished in about twelve minutes.

text: That's under a second per plan.
